title: The patriarchs are known only from Genesis
source_text: Πυνθανόμεθα γὰρ ἁπάντων τῶν χρωμένων ταῖς τοιαύταις τοῦ θεοῦ κατακλήσεσιν· εἴπατε ἡμῖν, ὦ οὗτοι, τίς ὁ Ἀβραὰμ καὶ πηλίκος ὁ Ἰσαὰκ καὶ ποίας δυνάμεως γέγονεν ὁ Ἰακὼβ, ὡς τὴν θεὸς προσηγορίαν ἁρμοζομένην αὐτῶν τῷ ὀνόματι τηλικάσδε ποιεῖν δυνάμεις; καὶ παρὰ τίνων μεμαθήκατε ἢ δύνασθε μαθεῖν τὰ περὶ τῶν ἀνδρῶν τούτων; τίς δὲ καὶ ἐπραγματεύσατο ἀναγράψαι τὴν περὶ αὐτοὺς ἱστορίαν, εἴτε καὶ αὐτόθεν σεμνύνουσαν ἐν ἀποῤῥήτοις τοὺς ἄνδρας εἴτε καὶ δι᾿ ὑπονοιῶν αἰνισσομένην τινὰ μεγάλα καὶ θαυμάσια τοῖς θεωρῆσαι αὐτὰ δυναμένοις; εἶτ᾿ ἐπὰν πυθομένων ἡμῶν μηδεὶς ἔχῃ παραστῆσαι ἀφ᾿ οἵας δή ποτε ἱστορίας, εἴτε Ἑλληνικῆς εἴτε καὶ βαρβαρικῆς ἢ οὐχ ἱστορίας ἀλλά τινος μυστικῆς ἀναγραφῆς τὰ περὶ τῶν ἀνδρῶν τούτων· ἡμεῖς προσοίσομεν τὴν ἐπιγεγραμμένην Γένεσιν, περιέχουσαν τὰς πράξεις τῶν ἀνδρῶν τούτων καὶ τοὺς τοῦ θεοῦ χρησμοὺς πρὸς αὐτοὺς, ἐροῦμέν τε ὅτι μή ποτε τὸ καὶ ὑφ᾿ ὑμῶν παραλαμβάνεσθαι τὰ ὀνόματα τῶν τριῶν τούτων γεναρχῶν τοῦ ἔθνους, τῇ ἐναργείᾳ καταλαμβανόντων οὐκ εὐκαταφρόνητα ἀνύεσθαι ἐκ τῆς κατεπικλήσεως αὐτῶν, παρίστησι τὸ θεῖον τῶν ἀνδρῶν; οὓς οὐδαμόθεν ἢ ἀπὸ τῶν ἱερῶν παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις βιβλίων παραλαμβάνομεν. ἀλλὰ γὰρ καὶ ὁ θεὸς τοῦ Ἰσραὴλ καὶ ὁ θεὸς τῶν Ἑβραίων καὶ ὁ θεὸς ὁ καταποντώσας ἐν τῇ ἐρυθρᾷ θαλάσσῃ τὸν Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέα καὶ τοὺς Αἰγυπτίους πολλάκις ὀνομάζεται παραλαμβανόμενος κατὰ δαιμόνων ἤ τινων πονηρῶν δυνάμεων. μανθάνομεν δὲ τὴν περὶ τὰ ὀνομαζόμενα ἱστορίαν καὶ τὴν τῶν ὀνομάτων ἑρμηνείαν ἀπὸ Ἑβραίων, τῶν τοῖς πατρίοις γράμμασι καὶ τῇ πατρίῳ διαλέκτῳ ταῦτα σεμνυνόντων καὶ διηγουμένων· πῶς οὖν Ἰουδαῖοι ταῦτ᾿ ἐπιχειρήσαντες ἑαυτοὺς γενεαλογεῖν ἀπὸ πρώτης σπορᾶς τούτων, οὓς γόητας καὶ πλανήτας ἀνθρώπους ὑπείληφεν εἶναι ὁ Κέλσος, ἀναισχύντως ἐπιχειροῦσιν ἑαυτοὺς καὶ τὴν ἀρχὴν αὑτῶν ἐπὶ τούτους ἀνάγειν, ὧν τὰ ὀνόματα Ἑβραϊκὰ τυγχάνοντα μαρτυρεῖ Ἑβραίοις, τὰ ἱερὰ αὐτῶν βιβλία ἐν Ἑβραίων ἔχουσι διαλέκτῳ καὶ γράμμασιν. ὅτι οἰκεῖόν ἐστι τὸ ἔθνος αὐτῶν τοῖς ἀνδράσι τούτοις; καὶ γὰρ μέχρι τοῦ δεῦρο τὰ Ἰουδαϊκὰ ὀνόματα, τῆς Ἑβραίων ἐχόμενα διαλέκτου. ἤτοι ἀπὸ τῶν γραμμάτων αὐτῶν ἐλήφθη ἢ καὶ ἁπαξαπλῶς ἀπὸ τῶν σημαινομένων ὑπὸ τῆς Ἑβραίων φωνῆς.
pass_a_gloss: For we inquire (πυνθανόμεθα) of all who use such invocations (κατακλήσεσιν) of God: Tell us, you there (ὦ οὗτοι), who is Abraham and how great (πηλίκος) Isaac and of what power (δυνάμεως) Jacob became, that the title (προσηγορίαν) 'God' fitted (ἁρμοζομένην) to their name does such great powers (δυνάμεις)? And from whom have you learned or can learn the things about these men? Who took the trouble (ἐπραγματεύσατο) to write up (ἀναγράψαι) the history (ἱστορίαν) about them, whether directly (αὐτόθεν) exalting (σεμνύνουσαν) the men in secret [writings] (ἐν ἀπορρήτοις) or through hidden meanings (δι' ὑπονοιῶν) hinting (αἰνισσομένην) great and wonderful things to those able to contemplate (θεωρῆσαι) them? Then when, on our asking, no one can present (παραστῆσαι) from what history at all, Greek or barbarian, or not history but some mystical record (μυστικῆς ἀναγραφῆς), the things about these men [come], we will bring forward (προσοίσομεν) the [book] entitled Genesis, containing the deeds (πράξεις) of these men and the oracles (χρησμούς) of God to them, and we will say: perhaps (μή ποτε) the fact that the names of these three founders (γεναρχῶν) of the nation are taken up (παραλαμβάνεσθαι) by you too, [you] grasping by plain evidence (τῇ ἐναργείᾳ καταλαμβανόντων) that not contemptible (οὐκ εὐκαταφρόνητα) things are achieved (ἀνύεσθαι) from invoking them (κατεπικλήσεως), establishes (παρίστησι) the divine [quality] (τὸ θεῖον) of the men? Whom we receive from nowhere but from the sacred books among the Jews. But indeed also 'the God of Israel' and 'the God of the Hebrews' and 'the God who drowned (καταποντώσας) in the Red Sea the king of the Egyptians and the Egyptians' is often named, being taken up against demons (δαιμόνων) or certain wicked powers (πονηρῶν δυνάμεων). We learn the history about the things named and the interpretation (ἑρμηνείαν) of the names from Hebrews, who in their ancestral letters (πατρίοις γράμμασι) and ancestral dialect (διαλέκτῳ) exalt and narrate these things. How then do Jews, having attempted to trace their genealogy (γενεαλογεῖν) from the first seed (σπορᾶς) of these, whom Celsus supposed (ὑπείληφεν) to be sorcerers (γόητας) and wanderers (πλανήτας), shamelessly (ἀναισχύντως) attempt to carry back (ἀνάγειν) themselves and their origin (ἀρχήν) to these, whose names, being Hebrew, testify (μαρτυρεῖ) to Hebrews, who have their sacred books in the Hebrew dialect and letters, that their nation is akin (οἰκεῖον) to these men? For even until now the Jewish names, holding to (ἐχόμενα) the Hebrew dialect, were taken either from their writings or simply (ἁπαξαπλῶς) from the things signified (σημαινομένων) by the Hebrew tongue (φωνῆς).
pass_b_english: For we put this question to all who use such invocations of God: “Tell us, sirs, who Abraham was, how great Isaac was, and what power Jacob had, that the title ‘God’, joined to their name, works such mighty deeds? From whom have you learned, or from whom can you learn, the facts about these men? And who took the trouble to write down their history, whether one that on its face exalts the men in secret writings, or one that by hidden meanings hints at great and wonderful things to those able to contemplate them?”

Then, when we ask and no one can show from what history at all the facts about these men come, whether Greek or barbarian, or not a history but some mystical record, we shall bring forward the book entitled Genesis, which contains the deeds of these men and God’s oracles to them. And we shall say: May it not be that the very fact that you too make use of the names of these three founders of the nation, because you see plainly that calling on them achieves results not to be despised, shows the divine character of these men? And we receive these men from no other source than the sacred books held among the Jews.

What is more, “the God of Israel” (Exodus 5:1), “the God of the Hebrews” (Exodus 3:18), and “the God who drowned the king of the Egyptians and the Egyptians in the Red Sea” (Exodus 14:27–28; 15:4) are often named and called upon against demons or certain wicked powers. And we learn the history of what is named, and the meaning of the names, from the Hebrews, who honour these things and tell of them in their ancestral writings and their ancestral language.

How then can the Jews, in trying to trace their descent from the first seed of these men, whom Celsus has supposed to be sorcerers and vagabonds, be shamelessly trying to trace themselves and their origin back to them, when the names of these men, being Hebrew, bear witness on behalf of the Hebrews, who have their sacred books in the Hebrew language and letters, that their nation is akin to these men? For even to this day the Jewish names, which belong to the Hebrew language, have been taken either from their writings or simply from what words mean in the Hebrew tongue.

choices.choice: 'praises the men in its plain words, among secret writings' -> 'on its face exalts the men in secret writings' (αὐτόθεν σεμνύνουσαν ἐν ἀπορρήτοις; removes the clumsy double phrase)
'take up the names' -> 'make use of the names' (παραλαμβάνεσθαι; less of a calque)
'find by plain experience' -> 'see plainly' (τῇ ἐναργείᾳ καταλαμβανόντων)

'we take these men from nowhere else than from the sacred books kept among the Jews' -> 'we receive these men from no other source than the sacred books held among the Jews' (παραλαμβάνομεν = receive)
'take pride in these things' -> 'honour these things' (active σεμνυνόντων with ταῦτα as object, not middle 'pride oneself'); clause order made natural
'carry back themselves and their origin to them' -> 'trace themselves and their origin back to them'
'bear witness to the Hebrews' -> 'bear witness on behalf of the Hebrews' (dative of advantage with μαρτυρεῖ)
Exodus 5:1, 3:18, 14:27-28, 15:4 checked against the verses (LXX 15:4 κατεπόντισεν ἐν ἐρυθρᾷ θαλάσσῃ); kept

Koetschau punctuates the opening inquiry and the 'μή ποτε ... παρίστησι' sentence as questions; μή ποτε with the indicative is Origen's tentative 'perhaps', rendered 'May it not be that ...?'. 'αὐτόθεν σεμνύνουσαν ἐν ἀπορρήτοις' contrasts praise in plain words (though within secret writings) with praise 'through hidden meanings' (δι' ὑπονοιῶν); rendered to keep that contrast. The genitive absolute 'τῇ ἐναργείᾳ καταλαμβανόντων' has no expressed subject; taken as the users of the names ('you'). The three invocation formulas are cited as allusions: 'God of Israel' (Exodus 5:1, a frequent title), 'God of the Hebrews' (Exodus 3:18; also 5:3), the drowning (LXX Exodus 15:4 κατεπόντισεν ἐν ἐρυθρᾷ θαλάσσῃ; narrative at 14:27–28). Celsus's 'πλάνων' (33) is 'deceivers'; Origen here paraphrases with 'πλανήτας' (wanderers), rendered 'vagabonds'. The final question ('How then ...?') is rhetorical: Origen means the Jewish claim is not shameless, because the Hebrew names prove the kinship. In the last sentence 'ἤτοι ... ἐλήφθη' is read as the main verb after the comma in the staged row.
